santos-vila-gilda-stilt-house-resettleme.title: Families Moved from Stilt Houses into Other Stilt Houses in Santos
santos-vila-gilda-stilt-house-resettleme.place: Vila Gilda and the Northwest Zone of Santos, São Paulo, Brazil
santos-vila-gilda-stilt-house-resettleme.point: The Dique Vila Gilda area of Santos, the stilt-house settlement on the Río dos Bugres from which the completion report says the families were moved. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give none.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-78070 (7807-BR) for the Santos Municipality Project (P104995). US$44.00 million, of which US$24.51 million was disbursed. Borrower the Municipality of Santos, with the guarantee of the Federative Republic of Brazil. Environmental category A. Approved 24 November 2009, effective 19 April 2010, restructured 1 June 2010, mid-term review 12 December 2012, closed 30 June 2015. Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) was triggered. The completion report ICR00003416, dated 7 June 2016 on its cover and carrying 23 September 2015 as the ICR date in its own data sheet, rated the outcome Unsatisfactory, risk to development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, borrower performance Unsatisfactory, quality at entry Unsatisfactory, quality of supervision Moderately Satisfactory, compliance with social safeguards Moderately Unsatisfactory, fiduciary compliance Unsatisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Moderately Unsatisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0020297 recorded the same four main ratings with no disagreement and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: Companhia de Habitação da Baixada Santista (COHAB-Santista)
companies.role: The executing agency for resettlement planning, slum upgrading and the move itself, and the builder of the housing complexes the families went to. The completion report describes it as the housing corporation established by the municipalities of Santos, São Vicente, Cubatão and Guarujá and operating under the COHAB By-Laws. It carried out a satisfaction survey of the residents of Vila Pelé II, in 2013 only (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2016).

companies.name: Municipality of Santos Secretariat of Government
companies.role: The implementing agency named in the completion report's data sheet. The Secretariat of Government, with support from COHAB-Santos under a specific agreement, took on the institutional responsibilities for resettlement. All resettlement activities were to be paid for out of the municipality's own counterpart funds, not the loan (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2016).

santos-vila-gilda-stilt-house-resettleme.community:
The project was meant to clear and upgrade stilt-house settlements on the Río dos Bugres in the northwest of Santos. The appraisal document of 29 October 2009 said about 2,400 families lived in those slums and about 1,100 of them, living in stilt houses, would be resettled into new houses.

By the time the loan closed on 30 June 2015, 712 families had been resettled: 480 to the Vila Pelé II housing complex in 2012, 160 to Caneleira IV Phase 1 in 2014 and 72 to Quadras 1 and 35 in Vila Gilda in 2014. The completion report puts that at 54 per cent of the number estimated in the resettlement action plan. Its resettlement summary table lists 1,324 housing units in total, 712 delivered by the end of the project and 612 still to come, including 520 at Caneleira IV Phase 2 then under construction. A further 88 families stayed where they were and were connected to water and sanitation. The project's own indicator was a package of municipal services for 2,400 households; 800 were reached.

In October 2011 the municipality told the Bank it had found 65 more affected families living in the works area, and agreed to pay for temporary housing until they could be moved to new houses, then planned for 2013. At a supervision mission in May 2012 the Bank team found that those families had instead been moved into other stilt houses, built by the municipality, "disregarding the RAP terms and the Bank Policies". The Bank demanded immediate action and the families were moved into temporary housing on housing allowances. The completion report states that by the end of the project "the 65 families, referred above, had not been properly resettled". Around 40 of them reached Caneleira IV Phase 1 late in 2015 and 23 more in May 2016. Three households were still waiting, with the municipality saying it meant to move them in the second half of 2016. Twenty-three families from Caminho São José were living on rent allowances when the project closed.

Three expropriation authorisations for the macro-drainage works were still outstanding at closing. The Bank asked in 2015 for an abbreviated resettlement plan for around 30 families occupying pumping station work sites and rejected the one submitted for not complying with its policy; the works were then suspended. A study finished in October 2015, after the project closed, recommended removing the stilt houses within 50 metres of the EEC7 pumping station and within 20 metres of the others. The completion report says the municipality has not yet estimated how many families that is. Geotechnical experts also found that excavation for part of the EEC7 culvert could cause structural damage to nearby buildings.

The completion report records that the 712 families moved from precarious stilt houses into apartment buildings and that the resettlement produced noticeable effects on poverty. None of the Phase I macro-drainage works were finished, so the project achieved little or no flood protection.
santos-vila-gilda-stilt-house-resettleme.displaced_label: families resettled by project closing, from the completion report's resettlement summary table
santos-vila-gilda-stilt-house-resettleme.displaced_note: ICIJ's table carries no displacement estimate for this project. The 712 is the completion report's count of families actually resettled. The appraisal document's 1,100 families is a plan figure, and the 2,400 families and 90,000 residents that appear in both the appraisal document and the evaluation review are counts of the population the project was meant to benefit, not of people moved.
santos-vila-gilda-stilt-house-resettleme.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2015 with US$24.51 million of US$44.00 million disbursed. Of the 1,324 housing units in the completion report's table, 612 were still to be delivered after closing. Three households from the group of 65 were still waiting to be moved when the report was written, and the Bank said it was continuing to follow up. The macro-drainage works were suspended, and the Bank told the municipality that all outstanding resettlement and expropriation matters had to be resolved under the resettlement action plan and its safeguard policy before any of the macro-drainage works could continue. The completion report rated the outcome Unsatisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

santos-vila-gilda-stilt-house-resettleme.confidence_note: Everything here rests on the Bank's own completion report on its own project, on the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report and on the appraisal document. No independent report on the 65 families was found. The documents do not name them, do not say where the stilt houses they were moved into stood, and do not say how long each family spent in temporary housing. Paragraph 61's footnote says 62 families had been resettled to Caneleira IV by the time the report was submitted, while Annex 4 gives "around 40" late in 2015 and 23 more in May 2016; the two are close but not the same, and the documents do not reconcile them. The number of families around the pumping stations is not estimated anywhere. The completion report's cover is dated 7 June 2016 and its data sheet gives the ICR date as 23 September 2015.

hopewell-road-land-taken-st-vincent.title: Land and Crops Taken for a Road Realignment Before the Resettlement Policy Applied
hopewell-road-land-taken-st-vincent.place: The Hopewell to Teviot road, between Hopewell and Richland Park, Mesopotamia valley, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
hopewell-road-land-taken-st-vincent.point: Richland Park, the settlement the remedial resettlement plan names as the far end of the Hopewell Road works, where the footpath used during construction met the main road. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give none and Hopewell itself is not in the gazetteer.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-48520 (4852-VC) for the Hurricane Tomas Emergency Recovery Project (P124939), SDR 3.30 million, US$5 million equivalent, of which SDR 3.11 million was disbursed. Borrower the Government of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines; implementing agency the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning. Lending instrument an emergency recovery loan, environmental category B. Approved 13 January 2011, effective 4 May 2011, mid-term review 22 January 2013, closed 31 December 2013. The project was restructured on 26 August 2013 to trigger Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), which had not been triggered at appraisal, after works had already taken land. The completion report ICR00003178, dated 30 June 2014 on its cover and 25 June 2014 in its data sheet, rated outcome Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR14666, posted 21 November 2014, agreed on outcome and on Bank performance but rated the risk to development outcome Significant rather than Moderate, because budgets for maintenance are generally inadequate and the line ministries' financial and capacity constraints are likely to hamper long-term maintenance.

companies.name: Ministry of Transport, Works, Urban Development and Local Government
companies.role: The ministry whose works took the land. The remedial plan records that it asked two landowners' permission to "cut Land" to realign a section of Hopewell Road, and that it and the contractors proceeded under national procedures that did not require them to inform the Central Planning Division, because the Bank's resettlement policy had not been triggered. Its Chief Engineer was the ministry's representative on the project, responsible for minor civil works and supervision and for defining the project area (Remedial Abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan, 14 March 2013; Resettlement Policy Framework, May 2013).

companies.name: Central Planning Division, Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning
companies.role: The unit inside the finance ministry that manages the project and its safeguards, and that notified the Bank of the land acquisition on 30 November 2012 once it had established the extent of the impacts. Under the policy framework it is responsible for procurement, financial management, monitoring and evaluation and payment of compensation (Remedial Abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan, 14 March 2013; Resettlement Policy Framework, May 2013).

hopewell-road-land-taken-st-vincent.community:
The project front-loaded repairs to infrastructure damaged by Hurricane Tomas, which struck in October 2010. The works picked for it were already known to the government and the Bank and were not expected to need any land acquisition, so the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy was not triggered and no resettlement framework or action plan existed.

During work on the Hopewell Road, soil erosion from heavy rainfall in October 2012 forced a change of engineering design, and the new design took land. A survey by the Lands and Surveys Department in September 2012 found encroachment on two properties, one on either side of the road: 3,064 square feet, which the plan puts at 40 per cent of that owner's assets, and 297 square feet, 1 per cent of the other's. Four people, in two families of two, were recorded as directly affected. The Central Planning Division told the Bank on 30 November 2012.

A Bank mission on 5 to 7 December 2012 visited the site, confirmed the encroachment and set out the steps for consulting and compensating the two owners. The same mission found the revised retaining-wall design inadequate, and on 22 December 2012 the Bank told the Director of Planning that the sub-project should be suspended until an acceptable design was produced. The Bank then began a restructuring to trigger the resettlement policy and asked the government to prepare a remedial abbreviated resettlement action plan and a resettlement policy framework.

The remedial plan, dated 14 March 2013, records what was agreed. Both owners chose cash. Compensation for crops was recorded as finalised on 5 March 2013, with values set from Ministry of Agriculture rates; payment for the temporary loss of use of agricultural land and of its productivity had been effected. The two payments for the land itself are recorded as "Awaiting payment", with June 2013 as the expected completion date, and the plan leaves the amounts as "value tbd". The plan notes that there is no provision for land-for-land compensation in the law of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, though it happens in practice case by case. The second owner's private pathway was used as a public right of way while the road was closed; no money was asked for, and instead five street lights were installed along 200 feet of road, officers were assigned from the Mesopotamia Police Station, and the public was urged to respect the property. In consultation the affected people "indicated the need for full and fair compensation of property and crops in a timely manner", and welcomed the gabion baskets supporting their land and crops and the benefit of a stabilised road.

The completion report puts the encroachment at 3,361 square feet in total and says it "did not have a substantial impact on the two affected land owners, nor on the community", and that the Bank, within two weeks of being told, sent a team that helped the government address the consultation and compensation and "effectively address[ed] the problem on the ground". At a second site, the Rillan Hill Community Centre, nearby residents had planted crops before works began; it was decided that no compensation was needed because the crops were harvested first.
hopewell-road-land-taken-st-vincent.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 4 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No one was relocated. The remedial resettlement plan records four people directly affected, in two families, each losing part of a plot.
hopewell-road-land-taken-st-vincent.killed_note: Twelve people were killed on 24 December 2013, a week before the project closed, by flash floods from a tropical trough system, which also displaced more than 225 people and caused damage the completion report puts at US$108.4 million. Those deaths were caused by the storm and not by the project or its works; they are recorded here because they fall inside the project's dates and inside the same valleys.
hopewell-road-land-taken-st-vincent.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2013 with SDR 3.11 million of SDR 3.30 million disbursed. No document found records the two payments for the land being made. The completion report, six months after the plan's own June 2013 deadline, says the Bank assisted the government in addressing the compensation and that the problem was effectively addressed, but gives no amounts and no date of payment. The remedial plan was disclosed in the country on 12 July 2013 and sent for public disclosure on 16 July 2013, and the project was restructured on 26 August 2013 to trigger the resettlement policy. The mid-term review recommended that the implementation unit's fiduciary and safeguard compliance be strengthened.

No independent report was found. cap-labadie-road-compensation-escrow.title: Eleven Landowners Still Unpaid When the Cap-Haïtien to Labadie Road Closed
cap-labadie-road-compensation-escrow.place: The Cap-Haïtien to Labadie road, Bande du Nord, Nord department, Haiti
cap-labadie-road-compensation-escrow.point: Labadie, the village at the far end of the road the resettlement plan covers; the works ran from Cap-Haïtien to the Labadie landing stage. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give none.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Grants IDA-H5510, IDA-H8120 and IDA-D1360 for the Infrastructure and Institutions Emergency Recovery Project (P120895), SDR 67.2 million, US$102.8 million equivalent in all: US$65 million under H5510, US$35 million under H8120 and US$2.8 million under D1360, of which US$100,526,845 was disbursed. Recipient the Republic of Haiti; implementing agency the Unité Centrale d'Exécution of the Ministry of Public Works, Transport and Communications. Environmental category A. Processed under OP 8.00, Rapid Response to Crises and Emergencies, after the January 2010 earthquake. Approved 18 March 2010, effective 23 April 2010, mid-term review 17 April 2012, original closing 30 June 2013, actual closing 29 June 2018. Additional financing was approved on 27 September 2012 under P130749 and a second on 10 November 2016 under P156049. Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP/BP 4.04), Pest Management (OP/BP 4.09) and Physical Resources (OP/BP 4.11) were triggered. The completion report ICR00004504, dated 27 December 2018, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and quality of monitoring and evaluation Modest; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021536 rated outcome and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, and its ratings table reports the completion report's Bank performance rating as Moderately Satisfactory where the report's own key ratings page says Satisfactory.

companies.name: Unité Centrale d'Exécution, Ministère des Travaux Publics, Transports et Communications
companies.role: The central implementation unit inside Haiti's public works ministry, named in the completion report's data sheet as the implementing agency and on the cover of the June 2018 resettlement plan as its author. It ran the resettlement, the census of affected people and the grievance mechanism, and continued to handle open cases under other Bank-financed projects after this one closed (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 December 2018; Plan d'Action de Réinstallation, June 2018).

companies.name: Comité Permanent d'Acquisitions à l'Amiable
companies.role: The Haitian government's land acquisition committee, which set the amounts owed to the people whose land was taken. The escrow account opened at the Banque de la République d'Haïti was provisioned in the amounts the committee set, as Haitian law provides (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 December 2018).

companies.name: Royal Caribbean
companies.role: The operator of the Labadie site. The June 2018 resettlement plan records that the extra kilometre of road added in September 2017, running to the Labadie landing stage, lies inside an existing right of way that is a concession from the Haitian state to Royal Caribbean, which operates the site, so no land along it was taken; an agreement was reached with the firm operating the site to move points of its metal fence where crossings were needed (Plan d'Action de Réinstallation, June 2018).

cap-labadie-road-compensation-escrow.community:
The project rebuilt government buildings and infrastructure after the earthquake of 12 January 2010. Resettlement action plans were prepared for five separate works, and the completion report says they resulted in "the relocation of 12 households, land acquisition for 136 households, and non-land economic displacement of 223 households".

The project's social safeguard rating was Satisfactory or Moderately Satisfactory until December 2017, when it was cut to Moderately Unsatisfactory because compensation for land taken from 19 affected people for the Cap Labadie road works had not been paid. They were to have been paid by the government in April 2017. Eight were paid before the scheduled closing date of 29 June 2018. For the remaining 11 the government opened an escrow account at the Banque de la République d'Haïti, provisioned in the amounts set by the government's land acquisition committee, and the accounts are to stay in place for 30 years "to ensure consistency and that obligations can be fulfilled at any time during this period". The resettlement plan for the road was updated and re-disclosed on 25 June 2018, four days before closing, and the project was then closed procedurally. The safeguard rating was put back up to Moderately Satisfactory to reflect the opening of the account.

The June 2018 plan sets out what the project owed along this road. Forty-three affected people whose trade was hit by the works were to get four months' income, 2,198,075.24 gourdes in the original plan, with the emergency works and the outfall canals expected to raise both the number of people and the amount. Twenty-two vulnerable people losing their housing were to get 25,800 gourdes each over twelve months, 567,600 gourdes in all. The owners of ten houses damaged by the project were to be paid three months of the house's rental value, 264,000 gourdes in all, to cover the repairs they had to make to go on living there. A food allowance of 3,600 gourdes a head over three months was set for 146 people in the families on the census, 1,576,800 gourdes in all. For one of the three plots needed for the Ducroix variant the owner asked to be paid in kind, land for land, and the construction plan was changed to avoid the other two plots because their owners could not be found; a design choice made in September 2017 avoided moving one house and its toilet, so those two people were no longer affected.

The project also ran a grievance mechanism with regular open consultations at each site. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that the project team told it that since the report was written 11 of the 19 affected people had been compensated and that the Bank was working with the authorities to compensate the remaining 8. That is a statement by staff rather than a document, and it reverses the split the completion report gives.
cap-labadie-road-compensation-escrow.displaced_label: households relocated, from the completion report's safeguards section
cap-labadie-road-compensation-escrow.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 582 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 12 households relocated, land acquisition for 136 households and non-land economic displacement of 223 households, and does not break those figures down by site.
cap-labadie-road-compensation-escrow.outcome: The grants closed on 29 June 2018, five years after the original closing date, with US$100,526,845 of US$102.8 million disbursed. Eleven of the nineteen people whose land was taken for the Cap Labadie road had not been paid, and their money sat in an escrow account at the central bank that is to remain available for 30 years. The Bank said its implementation support team had taken adequate precautions to bring the pending compensation to a close and that it would keep supervising open cases through other projects run by the same implementation unit. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

riohacha-wayuu-lagoon-resettlement.title: Wayuu Families Moved for Riohacha's Wastewater Lagoons and Left Without Electricity
riohacha-wayuu-lagoon-resettlement.place: El Arroyo, La Loma, Guayabito, Campo Alegre and Jirrawaika, around the El Encanto lagoon site, Riohacha, with works in Maicao and Uribia, La Guajira, Colombia
riohacha-wayuu-lagoon-resettlement.point: Riohacha, the municipality whose wastewater treatment lagoons the indigenous resettlement plan covers. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give none for the communities.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-74340 (7434-CO) for the La Guajira Water and Sanitation Infrastructure and Service Management Project (P096965), the first phase of an adaptable programme loan. US$90 million, revised to US$71,441,085 and that amount disbursed; total project cost US$108,161,085 against US$158.2 million planned, with the borrower providing US$36,720,000 of the US$50 million it had committed and the municipalities and local sources none of the US$18.2 million theirs. Approved 15 March 2007, effective 26 June 2007, mid-term review 1 November 2011, original closing 15 October 2011, actual closing 16 April 2018, after restructurings on 7 October 2011, 30 November 2011, 22 September 2015, 28 April 2016, 14 April 2017 and 12 October 2017. Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12), Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10), Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP 4.04), Cultural Property (OP 4.11), International Waterways (OP 7.50) and, from the November 2011 restructuring, Safety of Dams (OP 4.37) were triggered. The completion report ICR00004295, dated 15 October 2018, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, monitoring and evaluation Modest and safeguards Moderately Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021445 rated the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, disagreeing on the ground that "achievement against the project's objectives had significant shortcomings".

companies.name: Departamento de La Guajira
companies.role: The Colombian department that was the project's implementing agency, through a project implementation unit, and which signed the commitments made to the Wayuu communities. The completion report records that between 2013 and 2017 the department had seven governors, four elected and three interim; that one governor blocked the project's advance for four years in office; and that the following governor was arrested within a year on charges of conspiracy in the murder of political rivals and removed from office. The project was later run under a Temporary Administration (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 15 October 2018).

companies.name: Aguas de La Guajira S.A. E.S.P.
companies.role: The operator of the water supply system. The indigenous resettlement plan records that one of the two stated grounds for the temporary suspension of works contract No. 487 of 2001, on 22 December 2006, was that this operator had not met its commitment to supply water or to make the missing connections to the pipes already laid, which was one of the undertakings agreed with the community in the consultation meetings (Evaluación Social y Plan de Reasentamiento Indígena, June 2011).

companies.name: Fundación MANA
companies.role: The foundation that prepared the social evaluation and indigenous resettlement plan for the Riohacha wastewater system under Convenio 013 de 2009 with the department (Evaluación Social y Plan de Reasentamiento Indígena, June 2011).

riohacha-wayuu-lagoon-resettlement.community:
The project built water and sanitation works across La Guajira, a department whose rural population is largely Wayuu. Nine Wayuu communities stood in the direct area of influence of the wastewater treatment lagoons planned for Riohacha: 110 families and 518 people, by the census in the social evaluation and indigenous resettlement plan of June 2011. El Arroyo, La Loma and Campo Alegre were the largest.

Consultation on the lagoons ran for years. The plan records that works contract No. 487 of 2001 was suspended again on 22 December 2006 on two stated grounds: that the water operator had not met its commitment to supply water or complete the missing pipe connections, one of the undertakings agreed with the community, and that the indigenous families settled in the direct area of influence now had to be relocated. In December 2008 two meetings fixed commitments on housing and land purchase and the governor signed an undertaking for the definitive move of the families from the direct area. A list of commitments agreed between 2008 and 2010 includes school classrooms, a school canteen and sanitary units at La Loma, aqueduct pipes for La Loma and Guayabito on relocation, a reservoir, sixteen water tanks across sixteen communities, electricity networks for the relocated sections, a housing subsidy for seven families at Cuatro Bocas, and payment for improvements plus a housing improvement subsidy of up to 5,000,000 pesos each at 2,200,000 pesos a hectare for the land ceded.

The completion report of 15 October 2018 says the indigenous resettlement plan was 96 per cent complete at the time of the report and that the one outstanding commitment for the resettled houses was electrification, for which the government had budgeted but which the project did not deliver. It also records that the project "met significant resistance given that: (i) the municipalities/departments were not complying with the agreements established in the consultations; and (ii) with each consultation, the Project received more demands".

The Riohacha lagoon construction contract was signed in January 2016 and suspended in July 2016 at 9 per cent physical progress, first because of community opposition and then because a new national rule required an archaeological plan, which was approved only at the project's closure. In Maicao the lagoon "was stalled because of complications around the purchase of land for the community members who had to relocate due to the construction of the lagoon. The lagoon was 95% complete when the communities started stalling the works because they had not received any of the benefits agreed on through 'Consulta Previa'/IPP at that time." The land was bought in November 2017 and construction had still not resumed when the report was written. The Maicao lagoons were not financed by the project, which the report says limited the Bank's leverage over safeguard compliance; the project supported the social component there through the indigenous peoples plan.

The department's rural reservoir programme, ten reservoirs in Uribia, was conceived outside the project and brought into it in 2011; the report says it "was not in compliance with Bank safeguards" and that the Bank's team asked for construction to be suspended for want of technical support, and that by the end of the project all the reservoirs were operational and in compliance. The project gave 8,881 Wayuu people improved water sources against a target of 3,500, built ten reservoirs against a target of eight, and cut the time spent fetching water by more than four hours; nine of the ten reservoirs held water fit to drink, and in the tenth, Gran Vía, it did not. Rural sanitation reached 468 Wayuu residents in Riohacha and 112 in Maicao.
riohacha-wayuu-lagoon-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 518 for this project. That is to the person the figure in the June 2011 indigenous resettlement plan for the population of the nine Wayuu communities in the direct area of influence of the Riohacha lagoons: 110 families and 518 people. It is a count of people in the affected communities, not a count of people moved. No outcome document found counts the families actually relocated; the completion report refers to "the resettled houses" and says the plan was 96 per cent complete, without a number.
riohacha-wayuu-lagoon-resettlement.outcome: The loan closed on 16 April 2018, six and a half years after the original closing date, with US$71.4 million of US$90 million disbursed. The Riohacha lagoons were 9 per cent built and the contract suspended; the Maicao lagoon was 95 per cent built and stalled. Electrification of the houses the resettled Wayuu families had been given was still outstanding, with the money budgeted by the Temporary Water Administration or the authority in charge. The micro-aqueduct meant to improve water supply to indigenous communities under the Maicao plan stood at 80 per cent. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rated it Moderately Unsatisfactory.

rio-janeiro-rail-right-of-way-removals.title: Eighty-three Families Taken Out of the Rail Right of Way in Rio de Janeiro
rio-janeiro-rail-right-of-way-removals.place: Reta de Honório and Pilares on the Belford Roxo branch and Deodoro on the Deodoro branch, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
rio-janeiro-rail-right-of-way-removals.point: Pilares, Rio de Janeiro, one of the three clusters of dwellings inside the railway strip that the resettlement plan censused; the largest, Reta de Honório, is not in the gazetteer. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give none.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-81170 (8117-BR), the additional financing for the Upgrading and Greening the Rio de Janeiro Urban Rail System Project, carried under its own number P125630 and reported with the parent operation P111996. US$600 million approved as additional financing on 26 January 2012, revised to US$519,344,966, of which US$447,181,471 was disbursed; the loan and guarantee agreements are dated 5 September 2012. The parent loan was IBRD-77190 (7719-BR), US$211,700,000, of which US$211,580,612 was disbursed, with the agreements dated 24 September 2009. Borrower the State of Rio de Janeiro with the guarantee of the Federative Republic of Brazil. Parent approved 9 July 2009, effective 3 December 2009, mid-term review 15 June 2015, original closing 30 June 2014, actual closing 30 December 2022. Total project cost US$660,467,848, of which the borrower provided US$1,705,765 of the US$9,290,000 it had committed. Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Pest Management (OP/BP 4.09) were triggered at the start, and Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) were added under the revised project. The completion report, dated 27 June 2023, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0023561 agreed on outcome and Bank performance and found significant shortcomings in the monitoring and evaluation design.

companies.name: CENTRAL - Companhia Estadual de Engenharia de Transportes e Logistica
companies.role: The state transport engineering and logistics company named in the completion report's data sheet as the project's implementing agency. The report describes SuperVia as the private concessionaire and CENTRAL as the state company on the public side of the concession (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 June 2023).

companies.name: Secretaria de Transporte (SETRANS), Governo do Estado do Rio de Janeiro
companies.role: The state transport secretariat under whose Programa Estadual de Transporte PET 2 the resettlement plan was drawn up, and which guaranteed payment of indemnities at the value of the dwellings including every improvement built, on the basis of surveyors' reports (Plano de Reassentamento Involuntário, September 2011).

companies.name: SuperVia
companies.role: The private concessionaire that runs the Rio de Janeiro suburban rail system and carried out the works, named in the completion report as "SuperVia as the private concessionaire". The report records that the project's capacity to handle its impact mitigation challenges improved only once SuperVia's Environmental and Social Management Unit was given greater prominence and more resources, and that its semiannual environmental reports were often late and incomplete in the earlier years (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 June 2023).

rio-janeiro-rail-right-of-way-removals.community:
The project bought trains and upgraded the suburban rail system the State of Rio de Janeiro owns and SuperVia runs. Three clusters of houses stood inside the railway strip and had to go.

The state's resettlement plan of September 2011 censused every family occupying the strip and found 59 dwellings at Reta de Honório and 7 at Pilares on the Belford Roxo branch and 14 at Deodoro, 80 in all. Every registered dwelling was to be wholly affected. All were residential, all single-family with no shared occupancy and all occupied by the owner of the structure: the land itself is public and belongs to the State of Rio de Janeiro, so the plan recognises one category of affected person, the owner of the improvement who lives in it. Eighty compensation solutions were therefore required. Three options were offered: a housing unit built by the government, self-resettlement with a monitored indemnity, or payment of an indemnity at the value of the dwelling. The plan says 80 replacement housing units were to be provided to the required standard, and guarantees payment of indemnities at the value of the property including all improvements made, on the basis of surveyors' reports.

The completion report of 27 June 2023 says the project "had to resettle 83 families living in precarious conditions inside the railroad right-of-way on the Deodoro and Belford Roxo lines", that the resettlement action plan was drawn up and carried out in line with Bank guidelines, and that 70 families were rehoused and 13 took cash compensation. It calls the handling satisfactory and reports no significant safeguard concerns at closing.
rio-janeiro-rail-right-of-way-removals.displaced_label: families resettled, from the completion report of 27 June 2023
rio-janeiro-rail-right-of-way-removals.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 228 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The resettlement plan of September 2011 counted 80 households in three clusters inside the railway strip; the completion report says 83 families were resettled, 70 rehoused and 13 compensated in cash. Neither document explains the difference between 80 and 83.
rio-janeiro-rail-right-of-way-removals.outcome: The loans closed on 30 December 2022, eight and a half years after the original closing date, with US$658,762,083 of US$730,925,578 disbursed. The 83 families had been moved: 70 into new housing and 13 on cash compensation. The completion report also records that in 2016 the proceeds of several Bank loans to the State of Rio de Janeiro were confiscated under an injunction of the state judicial court, among them about US$1 million in this project's designated account, on a petition from civil servants who were not being paid on time because of the state's fiscal position; the Bank flagged the confiscation as non-compliance with the loan agreement and asked for an immediate refund, and in the end the state paid eligible expenditures directly and offset the arrested balance.

pernambuco-easement-payments-undocumente.title: Easement Payments to Twenty Landholders Undocumented When the Pernambuco Water Project Closed
pernambuco-easement-payments-undocumente.place: The Pirangi to Camevô water main and the Surubim sanitation system, with the Pirapama system in the Recife metropolitan region, Pernambuco, Brazil
pernambuco-easement-payments-undocumente.point: Surubim, Pernambuco, one of the two works the completion report names as the source of the unpaid easement fees. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give none.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-77780 for the Pernambuco Sustainable Water Project (P108654). US$190,000,000, all of it disbursed; total project cost US$433,082,131, of which the borrower provided US$243,082,131 against the US$220,000,000 originally committed and the US$340,200,000 revised. Borrower the State of Pernambuco. Approved 14 January 2010, effective 15 June 2010, mid-term review 8 April 2013, original closing 30 November 2015, actual closing 30 March 2020. Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11) and Safety of Dams (OP 4.37) were among the policies triggered. The completion report, dated 30 April 2021, rated outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Modest, and recorded that compliance with social safeguards, in the satisfactory range for most of the project, was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory at closing. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0022614 gave the same ratings and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: Companhia Pernambucana de Saneamento (COMPESA)
companies.role: The state water and sanitation utility that built and runs the works, and the body the Bank was holding to the post-closing safeguards action plan. The completion report records that the evidence of payment of the easement fees and the completion reports for four abbreviated resettlement action plans were under implementation and "closely monitored through monthly meetings with COMPESA". The report also notes that the utility's board had a lengthy decision-making process and that it lacked technically trained staff to review detailed engineering designs (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 April 2021).

companies.name: Secretaria de Recursos Hídricos, Government of Pernambuco
companies.role: The state water resources secretariat that housed the Project Coordination Unit responsible for procurement across the operation and for cross-support to the staff involved. The project was implemented by the state government and COMPESA together, with several other secretariats and state agencies as beneficiaries (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 April 2021).

pernambuco-easement-payments-undocumente.community:
The project expanded water supply and sewerage in the Recife metropolitan region and the Agreste of Pernambuco. Its social safeguard rating sat in the satisfactory range for most of its life and was cut to Moderately Unsatisfactory at closing "because of pending issues related to the documentation of the payment of easement fees for 20 landholders affected by the works of the Pirangi-Camevô water main and the Surubim sanitation system". The post-closing safeguards action plan the state agreed with the Bank requires evidence that those fees were paid, and completion reports for four abbreviated resettlement action plans that were still being carried out when the project ended.

On the rest of the land taken, the completion report says that "at project closing, the compensation payment processes related to the project's infrastructure (right of way) were still pending judgment, and there were a few gaps in documenting the processes and the related evidence".

The appraisal document of 30 November 2009 gives the only figures for the Pirapama water supply conveyance system, which was being built with the state's own counterpart money when the project was appraised and was the reason the Bank's resettlement policy was triggered. It says those works "have affected 294 families, including the resettlement of 202 families and 92 processes of acquisition of sections of land as right of way", and that the Bank evaluated the procedures already used and found them appropriate and consistent with its safeguards. It expected about 130 more families and eight small businesses to be resettled and 82 properties to be temporarily affected as the system went on, under a resettlement plan dated 11 July 2009 that the Bank found satisfactory on 17 July 2009. The completion report gives no outcome figure for any of these.

The completion report also says the project followed good practice on social risk management, complying with the resettlement and cultural property policies, hired a consultancy for each set of works to mobilise local communities and run a first-tier grievance channel alongside COMPESA's ombudsman, and managed the excavation works in the historic city of Olinda, a UNESCO World Heritage site, with archaeological specialists.
pernambuco-easement-payments-undocumente.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 220 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The only count of people resettled in any document found is in the appraisal document, which says the counterpart-financed Pirapama conveyance works had already affected 294 families, "including the resettlement of 202 families", before the loan was approved. That is an appraisal statement about works the loan did not finance, and no completion-report figure was found for it, so it is not carried as the project's own count.
pernambuco-easement-payments-undocumente.outcome: The loan closed on 30 March 2020, four years and four months after the original closing date, with all US$190 million disbursed. The easement payments to the twenty landholders were still undocumented, the right-of-way compensation processes were before the courts, and four abbreviated resettlement action plans had no completion reports. Those items went into a post-closing safeguards action plan monitored in monthly meetings with the utility, alongside corrective works for the Pirapama dam, which a dam safety classification puts at high risk, and for four flood contention dams whose construction was not finished. The completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group both rated the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory.
pernambuco-easement-payments-undocumente.conditions: The project triggered Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11) and Safety of Dams (OP 4.37). Safety of Dams work remained unfinished at closing: the completion report records that the Pirapama dam is classified as high risk, that recommendations from the Dam Safety Panel were not implemented inside the project's life, and that corrective works for it and for the four flood contention dams were carried into the post-closing safeguards action plan, with designs due in December 2020 and works in December 2021 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 April 2021).

manta-properties-taken-without-agreement.title: Properties Taken in Manta Before Any Agreement With Their Owners
manta-properties-taken-without-agreement.place: Vía Barbasquillo and the water and sanitation works of Manta, Manabí, Ecuador
manta-properties-taken-without-agreement.point: Barbasquillo, Manta, the area of the Vía Barbasquillo reconstruction for which the loan was restructured to pay sixteen landowners. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give none.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-82890 (8289-EC) for the Manta Public Services Improvement Project (P143996). US$100,000,000, revised to US$99,999,116 and that amount disbursed; the borrower's US$15,600,000 counterpart was revised to zero and none was provided. Borrower the Municipality of Manta with the guarantee of the Republic of Ecuador. Approved 8 August 2013, effective 18 July 2014, mid-term review 11 July 2016, original closing 30 June 2018, actual closing 31 December 2020, after six restructurings. Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12) was triggered because the water and sanitation works needed permanent and temporary land acquisition. The second-order restructuring of March 2019 required the Regional Vice President's approval, to allow loan proceeds to be spent on land acquisition to compensate sixteen landowners affected by the reconstruction of Vía Barbasquillo; the restructuring of June 2020 reallocated funds between disbursement categories "to complete compensation payments due to land acquisition". The completion report, dated 30 November 2021, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, monitoring and evaluation Modest, and social safeguards Moderately Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0022845 gave the same ratings and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: Gobierno Autónomo Descentralizado Municipal del Cantón Manta
companies.role: The municipality that borrowed and implemented, through a project implementation unit that had one social specialist and, the completion report says, low capacity. The report records that the unit's legal team, which prepared the resolutions and carried out the land acquisition, feared future problems with the Comptroller if it followed the Bank's resettlement policy instead of national law, so it "tended to delay decision making, did not implement agreements, and avoided compliance with OP 4.12". It had never run a project financed by a multilateral bank. The municipality had three different mayors and the unit four different leaders over the project's life, and the report records difficulties caused by political actors who wanted to manipulate the project's procurement (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 November 2021).

companies.name: Empresa Pública Aguas de Manta (EPAM)
companies.role: The municipal water and sanitation company that operates the systems the project built and extended. The completion report quotes its general manager on the effect of the loan on service quality and reports that the project updated and brought into operation the company's commercial system (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 November 2021).

manta-properties-taken-without-agreement.community:
The project rebuilt water, sewerage and street infrastructure in Manta, on the coast of Manabí, which was hit by a magnitude 7.8 earthquake in April 2016.

The Bank's resettlement policy was triggered because the works needed land, permanently and temporarily. The implementation unit prepared a resettlement policy framework in 2016 to deal with people losing access to land, assets or income. The completion report states what happened next: "The PIU's low capacity as well as a high-level of political involvement in the Project contributed to issues with the initial land acquisition processes. Several properties were taken without having all the required permits or without having reached agreements with the owners. This situation occurred for almost a year at the beginning of the Project; the Bank presented its non-conformities in different documents, and the Borrower satisfactorily complied with the required processes."

In March 2019 the Bank restructured the loan, with the approval of its Regional Vice President, so that loan money could be used to compensate sixteen landowners whose land was taken for the reconstruction of Vía Barbasquillo. In June 2020, six months before the loan closed, a further restructuring moved money between disbursement categories "to complete compensation payments due to land acquisition".

The completion report's lessons set out why the compensation went wrong. Ecuadorian regulation "does not reach the full replacement cost required by OP 4.12 for land acquisition". The implementation unit was reluctant to go against national rules even though the Bank's rules take precedence in this kind of project, and its legal team was afraid of trouble with the Comptroller if it followed the Bank's policy, so it delayed decisions, did not implement agreements and avoided complying with the policy. The Bank "had to escalate this issue to the highest level of management to bring about change and ensure compliance", and an agreement signed with the Comptroller proved useful in getting compliance.

The report says the project finished in compliance with all the requirements of the Bank's Environmental and Social Framework despite these difficulties. The project's rehabilitation works benefited 15,740 household sewerage connections, beating the restructured target of 15,500 by 2 per cent and missing the original target of 17,318 by 9 per cent.
manta-properties-taken-without-agreement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 150 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document found counts anyone relocated. The only figures are the sixteen landowners whose land was taken for the Vía Barbasquillo reconstruction and the "several properties" the completion report says were taken without the required permits or without agreement with the owners.
manta-properties-taken-without-agreement.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2020, two and a half years after the original date, with almost all of the US$100 million disbursed. Compensation payments for land acquisition were still being completed six months before closing, and the completion report says the project finished in compliance with the Bank's social requirements, with a social safeguard rating of Moderately Satisfactory. The report's own lesson is that projects in countries whose national rules fall short of replacement cost should carry a separate budget line for land acquisition and resettlement from the start. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

el-alto-avenue-land-paid-for-afterwards.title: Land Taken for El Alto's Avenues and Paid For Years Afterwards
el-alto-avenue-land-paid-for-afterwards.place: Avenida Santa Vera Cruz in Districts 5 and 6 and Avenida Litoral in the Urbanización El Paraíso, El Alto, Bolivia
el-alto-avenue-land-paid-for-afterwards.point: Avenida Santa Vera Cruz, El Alto, the avenue whose paving the abbreviated resettlement plan covers. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap; the Bank documents give none.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-42470 (4247-BO) and IDA-51680 (5168-BO) for the Bolivia Urban Infrastructure Project (P083979). US$54,000,000 in all, US$30,000,000 under the first credit and US$24,000,000 under the additional financing, of which US$46,218,927 was disbursed. Borrower the Plurinational State of Bolivia. Approved 21 November 2006, effective 12 September 2007, mid-term review 25 September 2009, original closing 30 November 2010, actual closing 30 September 2017, after restructurings beginning 15 August 2010. Component 1 upgraded neighbourhoods in La Paz, Component 2 urban transport in El Alto and Component 3 sewerage in Santa Cruz. Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11) were triggered; the appraisal document said no resettlement was expected but that works under Components 1 and 2 might in very limited cases entail population displacement. The completion report, dated 26 March 2018, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Modest, and rated compliance with environmental safeguards Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021219 gave the same ratings with no disagreement recorded and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: Gobierno Autónomo Municipal de El Alto
companies.role: The municipality that carried out the El Alto urban transport component. The completion report records that it prepared a conflict management plan and said that documentation of a "voluntary cession of land" had been planned before the project identification phase but was carried out after the Bank became involved, and that it then prepared an abbreviated resettlement plan for retroactive, in-kind compensation. It is left in charge of the one case unresolved at closing (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 March 2018).

companies.name: Gobierno Autónomo Municipal de La Paz
companies.role: The municipality that ran the neighbourhood upgrading component under its Programa Barrios de Verdad. The completion report records that all adverse impacts on third parties in La Paz were dealt with by changes in design, repositioning front walls and small structures such as stairs at the entrances of houses, and that the city prepared an abbreviated resettlement plan establishing in-kind replacement of perimeter walls, entrance stairs and railings (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 March 2018).

el-alto-avenue-land-paid-for-afterwards.community:
The project paved avenues in El Alto, upgraded poor neighbourhoods in La Paz and extended sewerage in Santa Cruz.

On the El Alto avenues the land had already been handed over before the Bank arrived. The completion report says the municipality "prepared a Conflict Management Plan and indicated that documentation of a 'voluntary cession of land' had been planned before the PP's identification phase, but had been carried out after the Bank's involvement in project identification". The municipality then prepared an abbreviated resettlement plan "to provide retroactive, in-kind compensation to 6 property owners for the land they had ceded for the construction of 'Av. Santa Vera Cruz - Tramo 1'. Five of the six cases were solved at the end of the Project, and property owners obtained legal titles for their lots (with their new square footage). Only one case is pending", left with the El Alto municipal government, which expected to finish it within a couple of months.

The retroactive plan for Avenida Litoral, dated 10 November 2010, describes the same pattern on another avenue. Eleven residents of the Urbanización El Paraíso ceded the land needed for a road line of 48.5 metres, which the municipality had fixed in 2003, two years before the Bank's first identification mission in April 2005. All eleven plots were partially affected and none wholly. No valuation was carried out, the plan says, because the transfer was treated as the return of municipal land. Because the areas ceded came to more than 10 per cent of each plot, the Bank's policy required retroactive compensation, and the plan says the Bank was examining whether the 2003 agreement had legal force, whether its signatories were still the owners, and whether they still agreed with what they had signed, since "the areas ceded by the residents are greater than 10%, which may imply an impact of great magnitude for the owners". Of the eleven signatories, the plan notes, one had died, one was a new owner, and for one the original title documents were missing and that owner's willingness to sign the updated agreement had still to be established.

The abbreviated resettlement plan for Avenida Santa Vera Cruz, dated July 2013, counted 137 properties built over the municipal line. One hundred and twenty-eight of them encroached on part of the pavement without blocking it and were not treated as affected; nine blocked the pavement and part of the carriageway and had to pull back to the line. One of the nine owners waived the entitlement and said he would move back at his own expense, leaving eight eligible. In every case the loss was partial and nobody had to move elsewhere. The plan also counted the trades along the avenue: 44 shops selling building materials and daily food, and 54 vehicles belonging to hauliers carrying sand, stone and building materials. Neither group was to get any material compensation. The shops were promised crossings so customers could still reach them; the hauliers were promised help in moving to a nearby part of the avenue where they could work in much the same way.
el-alto-avenue-land-paid-for-afterwards.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 148 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document found counts anyone relocated, and both plans say the impacts were partial and that no one had to move to another site. The completion report counts six property owners given retroactive compensation on Avenida Santa Vera Cruz Tramo 1, of whom five were settled and one was not; the July 2013 plan for the same avenue counts eight eligible affected properties out of nine required to pull back to the municipal line, and the November 2010 plan for Avenida Litoral counts eleven. Neither document explains the difference between six and eight.
el-alto-avenue-land-paid-for-afterwards.outcome: The credits closed on 30 September 2017, nearly seven years after the original closing date, with US$46.2 million of US$54 million disbursed. Five of the six owners on Avenida Santa Vera Cruz Tramo 1 had been compensated in kind and held legal title to their plots at their new size. One case was unresolved and left with the El Alto municipal government. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

el-alto-avenue-land-paid-for-afterwards.confidence_note: Everything rests on the Bank's own completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it and the two abbreviated resettlement plans the municipality wrote for the Bank. No independent source on these land cessions was found. The documents do not say what the one unresolved owner was owed or whether it has since been settled: the completion report's footnote records only that the municipality expects to finish the case "in the next couple of months". The counts do not line up: the completion report gives six owners on Tramo 1, the July 2013 plan gives eight eligible out of nine required to pull back, and the November 2010 plan for Avenida Litoral gives eleven. The Avenida Litoral plan says no valuation was done because the land was treated as a return of municipal property, so there is no figure for what was taken. Whether the shops and hauliers lost trade, and how much, is not recorded in any outcome document; the plan only says they would get no material compensation.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: The resettlement plan for the accident is disclosed in the Bank's document archive as RP591, filed under the São Paulo Metro Line 4 Project Additional Financing (P105959), whose approval ICIJ's table records as 8 April 2008. No completion report and no evaluation review filed under that number could be reached, and no Bank document found for it states a loan number or an amount. The appraisal document for the São Paulo Metro Line 5 Project (P116170), dated 3 March 2010, records that the State of São Paulo had been managing Metro Line 4 Phases 1 and 2 as a Bank Category A project requiring Environmental Assessment and Involuntary Resettlement policies, that "during project implementation of Line 4 (Phase 1) in January 2007, an accident occurred in which 7 people died due to the collapse of the tunnel at Pinheiros station which was being excavated", and that this "led to additional involuntary resettlement due to damage to homes and to the need to evacuate other dwellings and businesses until their safety could be assured". The same document says the Bank reviewed the design and implementation of the required resettlement and found it satisfactory, and that "the resettlement and compensation of affected parties is now complete, with no cases pending". It also lists the lessons of the Pinheiros accident among the measures to be taken into account on Line 5.

pinheiros-station-collapse-sao-paulo.community:
On 12 January 2007 the ground gave way at the works for the future Pinheiros station of Line 4-Amarela of the São Paulo metro. Seven people were killed. A resettlement plan setting out the position as at 31 October 2007, published in December 2007 and disclosed in the World Bank's archive as RP591 under the Line 4 additional financing, records what the accident did to the neighbourhood.

Ninety-nine properties were affected, on five streets: 42 on Rua Gilberto Sabino, 30 on Rua Capri, 18 on Rua Conselheiro Pereira Pinto, 7 on Rua Eugênio de Medeiros and 2 on Rua Amaro Cavalheiro. Fifty-eight were residential, 25 commercial, 6 mixed with work carried on at home, 9 unoccupied and 1 other. Twelve were condemned and six demolished; six were sealed off, 17 were still under analysis, 34 were released with a city structural report, 10 released with reservations, 11 released quickly as minimal impact and 3 had no city intervention.

Two hundred and seventy-one people were affected, not counting the owners who did not live in the properties, of whom there were 57. The census counted 134 women and 137 men, 42 people over 65, 52 with chronic illness and 2 with disabilities. Forty-three of the households were tenants paying rent, 10 occupied properties lent to them, 36 were resident owners and one entry is recorded as squatters.

Seven deaths are recorded. Eight indemnity agreements were signed for them, because in one case the victim had two families.

Of the 99 properties, nine were empty on the day of the accident and four stayed occupied with minimal impact. Eighty cases had been settled by 31 October 2007, producing 34 returns to the original property, 59 resettlement addresses and 8 atypical cases with neither a return nor a resettlement; the plan notes that some occupants split between several addresses after resettlement. Six cases were still awaiting negotiation: three families lodged only in hotels, one split between a hotel and a relative's house, and two lodged with relatives with their cases in litigation. The hotels used were the George V, the Golden Tower and the New Citi. The agreements signed covered indemnity for death, moral and material damages, material damages, damages for the dissolution of a tenancy, lost profits together with moral and material damages, lost profits with other indemnities, and other indemnities.

On 16 February 2024 the São Paulo state court published a first-instance decision in case 0009559-70.2010.8.26.0053, given by the 5th Public Treasury Court of the state capital, holding six people and seven companies liable for administrative improbity over the collapse. The six lost any public office they held, had their political rights suspended for five years, were fined at twice the damage, to be quantified later, and were barred for five years from contracting with the public sector or receiving public benefits or tax incentives; the seven companies were fined on the same basis and barred on the same terms. The court ordered R$6.5 million paid to the São Paulo Metrô, the value of the contract, plus R$232 million in collective moral damages and R$1.2 million in diffuse property damages. The decision can be appealed. The court's notice names neither the individuals nor the companies.
pinheiros-station-collapse-sao-paulo.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 129 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The resettlement plan counts 271 people affected, excluding 57 owners who did not live in the properties, across 99 properties. Its summary gives 59 resettlement addresses out of 80 settled cases, alongside 34 returns to the original property and 8 atypical cases, and notes that some occupants split between several addresses after resettlement, so the 59 cannot be read as a count of 59 households. No figure is carried here as a count of households relocated.
pinheiros-station-collapse-sao-paulo.outcome: The resettlement plan's position at 31 October 2007 was 80 of 99 cases settled and six still in negotiation, two of those in litigation. The appraisal document for Line 5, dated 3 March 2010, says the resettlement and compensation of the affected parties was complete with no cases pending, and that the Bank had reviewed the design and implementation of the resettlement and found it satisfactory. The São Paulo state court's improbity judgment of February 2024, seventeen years after the collapse, holds six people and seven companies liable and orders R$239.7 million in payments; it is subject to appeal.
