pinheiros-station-collapse-sao-paulo.confidence_note: The death toll, the property figures and the household census come from the resettlement plan the metro company published in December 2007 and disclosed through the Bank's archive, which reports the position as at 31 October 2007 and nothing later. The São Paulo state court's own notice of 16 February 2024 carries the improbity decision, the case number and the sums ordered, but names none of the six people or seven companies held liable, and the decision is a first-instance one that can be appealed. No completion report or evaluation review filed under the Line 4 additional financing could be reached, so no Bank document found states the loan number or the amount of that operation, and the link to the lender rests on the plan's filing under that project number and on the Line 5 appraisal document's account of the accident during Line 4 Phase 1. The plan's summary figures do not add up to a household count: 34 returns plus 59 resettlement addresses plus 8 atypical cases comes to 101 from 80 settled cases, which the plan explains by occupants splitting between several addresses. The Line 5 appraisal document, written three years later, says the resettlement and compensation were complete with no cases pending.

recife-capibaribe-resettlement-still-pen.drop_reason: No document records anyone relocated. The completion report for the Recife Urban Development and Social Inclusion Project (ICR3043, 14 April 2014) says at paragraph 44 that "at the time of Loan Closing the resettlement of about 760 families affected by the construction of the road system and bridge over the Capibaribe River, and integrated urban upgrading and macro-drainage works was still pending", and at paragraph 45 that the Bank "will continue supervising the resettlement of these 763 families" because the works will not be finished until June 2018. That is a count of families affected and awaiting a move, which the forward rule treats as a drop. Checked in the outcome documents: Table 2 of the same report, "Pending Works after Project Closing", lists the resettlement of 403 families for the Casarao do Barbalho housing complex and "at most 360 families" for the road and bridge as future events, both financed by national programmes (PAC and Minha Casa Minha Vida) rather than by the loan, and records that the borrower was revising the bridge designs to reduce the number of affected people and to spare a school. PDO indicator 5, resettled ZEIS households with legal land tenure, is reported as "Loan closed before relevant project components were completed. (TARGET NOT MET)" against a target of 100 per cent. The Independent Evaluation Group's review (ICRR14352) repeats the same 760 figure as a risk that "remains", adds nothing, and records no resettlement carried out. The only completed social output in the report is 581 people trained at a rehabilitated job centre. The appraisal document's 1,453 families to be resettled is a plan figure; the resettlement framework of 1 December 2005 says the plan establishing how many families are to be relocated would be executed in the project's first year, and no such count appears in an outcome document. Nothing in either outcome document records compensation unpaid, land taken, a death, an injury, an arrest or a livelihood lost.

corn-island-wetland-resettlement.drop_reason: Ten families, 57 people, were moved, but no document records a loss on top of the move, and the destination is better than the origin on the face of the documents. The completion report (30 December 2018) says at paragraph 65 that "a total of 10 families (57 people) were resettled from living within the wetlands recharge areas and a resettlement plan was reviewed by Bank social development specialists and implemented at the beginning of the project implementation", that the move freed wetland that recharges the island's aquifer, and that "no other resettlement or indigenous peoples' issues occurred during implementation". Checked in the outcome documents: the report's output list records "wetland recharge areas in Corn Islands recovered from human establishments" as achieved, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review (28 February 2019) says the project complied with all social and environmental safeguards and describes the plan without reporting any grievance or shortfall. The resettlement plan itself (Proyecto de Reasentamiento Poblacional Humedal Coe, Barrio Brig Bay No. 1, May 2012) is explicit on what the families got: the ten houses they were leaving were valued at an average of 25,000 córdobas each and the new houses at 178,000 córdobas each, "el costo de las nuevas viviendas superan en 600% al precio de avalúo de las viviendas del humedal"; they held neither title nor land in the wetland and were to be given title to the new plot by the municipality; the municipality was to move their belongings; and "hasta el momento, ninguna persona de las 10 familias ha mostrado resistencia u objeción al reasentamiento". The plan also records that in the wetland they were exposed to flooding and respiratory illness. ICIJ's estimate of 57 for this project is the same 57 people. Under the round 19 limit on limb (a) a relocation out of a hazard zone with secure tenure at the destination and no recorded loss is not a case.

machu-picchu-pueblo-resettlement-dropped.drop_reason: The resettlement never happened. The appraisal document of 12 August 2004 said "The project has identified 60 families in Machu Picchu Pueblo that reside outside town boundaries on land extremely vulnerable to landslides. These families will be resettled within the pueblo or at an acceptable location identified outside the town", with a resettlement action plan in Annex 17 and a separate plan filed for 60 urban families. Checked in the outcome documents: the completion report of 19 December 2011 says "No resettlement in Machu Picchu Pueblo was to be carried out as analysis of risk financed with a GFDRR grant suggested the entire town was at risk, not just the 60 families originally identified", that the activity was changed to an early warning system and other risk management measures, and at paragraph 38 that "the resettlement safeguard was triggered originally but then detriggered during Project restructuring". Paragraph 51 repeats that "although the original aim was to relocate 60 households, this was dropped". The Independent Evaluation Group's review confirms that the resettlement policy was no longer triggered and that the housing construction activity was re-oriented to the early warning design. The only harm language in the documents is in the appraisal document's description of conditions before the project: falling stones that had struck the train, injuring three tourists, one of whom died of a heart attack, and the loss of life and property in Machu Picchu Pueblo in the floods that preceded the project. Those predate the project and were not caused by it. The outcome documents record no compensation unpaid, no land taken, no death, no injury and no arrest; the one social conflict they report is local opposition to any solution that would move the train station, which was not built.

rio-bogota-el-porvenir-resettlement.drop_reason: Families were moved, but every document records the destination as better than the origin and no loss on top of the move. The completion report of 31 May 2023 says at paragraph 101 and in its results narrative that "105 families from the low-income, flood-prone urban area of El Porvenir in the Mosquera municipality were successfully resettled to a new neighborhood with improved living conditions, and 19 families opted for individual resettlement". Checked in the outcome documents: paragraph 103 gives the detail. El Porvenir was 124 buildings; the site of the move was agreed with the settlers in a consultation lasting more than two years; it was close enough to keep support networks, schooling and access to health and transport; "since the settlers did not own the land but did own the improvements, the resettlement implied that they now owned the land and the houses built"; a warehouse was built for the residents who make a living from recycling, 25 homes with 51 people; a park, green areas and a nursery were built beside the new settlement; a visit three years later found the houses well kept and extended; and "no complaints were filed during and after the resettlement process". On the river works, paragraph 102 says the purchase of about 320 strips of land along the river "did not imply transfer of people or limitations on existing activities; nor did it imply crop elimination" and that "the entire process was voluntary and did not require coercive actions, let alone the use of force". The Inspection Panel complaint of 2016 concerned the design of the El Salitre wastewater plant, not the resettlement: paragraph 92 records that the Panel did not recommend an investigation, and the Panel's nine recommendations, which led to a design change preserving a wetland, had all been met by 2020. Two figures in the report do not match - the component description at page 12 lists "land acquisition, resettlement, and compensation of 188 households" while the outcome narrative gives 105 plus 19 - and the report does not reconcile them. Searches of Colombian sources in Spanish for the El Porvenir resettlement in Mosquera returned only World Bank blog posts. This is the same shape as the Bogotá Disaster Vulnerability Reduction case that round 19 dropped.

cordoba-road-right-of-way-land-donations.drop_reason: Land was taken for right of way, but no document records a loss to anyone, and both outcome documents record the transfers as voluntary donations with compensation in kind. The completion report of 21 April 2014 says at section 2.4.3 that "a total of 102 properties were affected by RoW acquisition. The loss of land suffered by the landowners was minor. In all cases, the land taken represents less than 7% of the total area of the property affected. The affected properties were large (between 500 and 10,000 hectares)", that landowners received compensation in kind such as new fencing and improved entrances, that "RoW acquisition did not cause physical displacement (relocation)", and that the landowners who donated land chose to do so and could have asked for expropriation instead: one did, and was compensated under an amicable agreement, the avenimiento. The report's footnote 17 says the Bank's resettlement policy "does not apply to the land donations that took place in the context of this project, given their voluntary nature" and applies only to that single expropriation. Checked in the outcome documents: the Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats those figures and adds that "the project relied to a considerable extent (the precise percentage is unknown) on voluntary donations of land", without finding a shortfall; it records no grievance, no unpaid compensation and no displacement. The one relocation the project might have caused, of informal vendors beside a new bridge over the Río Los Reartes, was avoided by changing the bridge's design and location. The harm language the pre-extraction surfaced for this row is road-safety material: the appraisal document's national road fatality rates and the completion report's claim of a fall in accidents and deaths after the road safety plan. Neither is harm by the project.

sao-paulo-metro-line-5-expropriations.drop_reason: The land acquisition is counted in structures, not people, and no document records a loss to anyone; and the Bank did not finance the works that took the land. The completion report of 22 June 2021 says at paragraph 77 that the project "triggered OP 4.12 Involuntary Resettlement requiring land acquisition affecting 355 buildings (239 housing units and 116 commercial units)", that a resettlement action plan was prepared, not objected to by the Bank and "fully implemented until completion in 2015", that most affected people received cash compensation, and that 48 vulnerable families could choose between cash, a housing voucher and a new unit in a complex built by the state housing company. Owners of commercial premises were compensated in cash and told they could claim for foregone profits. In 2015 the metro company surveyed 176 affected people about their new homes, their takings and their neighbourhoods, and it ran a grievance mechanism through which more than 3,000 communications were received and redressed. The only adverse note is paragraph 67: "Resettlement for the civil works of Line 5 had a few emblematic cases in which residents or businesses resisted relocation in spite of the mutually beneficial solutions that were offered", with no count and no loss attached. A structure count cannot carry the displacement field, which on this map holds people, households or families. Checked in the outcome documents: the Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the 355 buildings and the compensation options and records no shortfall; its statement that the project complied with the resettlement policy is attributed to a project team email of 17 August 2021, not to a document. Separately, the works that took the land were not financed by this credit: paragraph 60(a) of the completion report says "the World Bank-financed components of Line 5 are the acquisition of trains and the installation of CBTC systems and platform doors", and the appraisal document of 3 March 2010 says the civil works "will be financed and executed by the Borrower" and that construction accident risk "is an indirect risk because Bank is not involved in the civil works". The seven deaths at the Pinheiros station collapse of January 2007, which the Line 5 appraisal document describes, belong to Line 4 and are carried as a separate case.
